subject: moonBase
pitch:
Category: Diorama.
Subject: small moon base with dome and antenna.
Style: 1950s retro-futurism.
reasoning:
I'm planning a 1950s retro-futurism moon base diorama with a dome and antenna as a static scenery model, deciding whether to skip joints entirely or add one rotating radar dish joint for subtle animation.

I'm settling on a lunar surface disc as the base plate, with a central glass dome, cylindrical habitat modules, an antenna tower with a lattice mast and dish, and considering adding a small retro fin-tailed rocket to complete the scene.

I'm also adding modest extras like solar panels, fuel tanks, an airlock tunnel, and a ladder, keeping the part budget around 180-340 parts and 5-12 textures since I can't test the build. For scale I'm going with roughly a 1.2 m diorama, base radius 0.6, dome radius 0.22, antenna height 0.55, all in meters at tabletop scale, with a retro palette of teal, cream, coral, and mustard against grey-beige lunar ground. Since true transparency isn't available, I'm working out how to fake the glass dome — maybe ribbed framing with alpha-tested card textures standing in for glass panes.

Thinking further, I'm leaning toward a see-through lattice dome built from meridian ribs and latitude rings rather than a solid lathe shape, since that would let me reveal a tiny interior scene inside — a little tree, a lamp, a small table — which adds charm worth the extra part cost.

I'll go with a solid cream-paneled drum base topped by an open lattice cap with ribs, like a greenhouse frame, letting the glowing garden and tree show through the gaps rather than trying to fake translucent glass panes.

That works well since back faces get culled, so looking through the dome shows nothing on the far side as desired — it's effectively a see-through glass dome with painted ribs and highlights visible only from outside. I'm mapping the texture's UV coordinates around the hemisphere, matching the geometry's theta range so the drawing wraps correctly over the kept portion.

Writing SVG texture code...

Settling on 24 width segments and 8 height segments with flat shading for that faceted glass look. I'm also considering adding real 3D meridian ribs via arc sweeps from base to top, rotating points around a horizontal axis to give physical relief rather than just texture lines.

Working out rib rotation math...

The tubes converge at top where I'll add a finial cap at small radius. For texture, I'm planning latitude rings at a few levels plus diagonal brace lines between ribs, carefully mapping UV coordinates so diagonals connect rib to rib without needing to align with the 3D meridians themselves.

I'm computing the sphere's parametric coordinates and matching rib direction angles to the UV seam position to make sure the geometry lines up correctly.

Latitude rings in the texture can map directly from v fractions without needing full 3D math. I'm also considering whether the glass dome needs any tint or pane fill to feel more like glass, but leaning toward keeping it transparent with just glints for effect.

For the interior, I'm sketching a retro biodome scene: three small trees, a central glowing "atom lamp" with orbiting rings, and a bench, all visible through the glass. The dome sits on a short cylindrical drum base with portholes and a piped band, and the floor inside shows a teal checker pattern painted procedurally based on position.

Now I'm working out the overall layout in meters—a moon-disc ground acting as a diorama pedestal with a turquoise-trimmed rim, topped by an engraved plaque reading "LUNA STATION 1" rendered with SVG text. I'm shaping the plinth as a lathe profile with flat segments to give it a faceted 1950s look.

For the lunar surface sitting on the plinth, I'm planning a lumpy lathed disc with mottled grey paint, and working out how to fake craters using raised rims and darker bowl-shaped discs rather than literal depressions in the geometry.

Checking the polygon doesn't self-intersect and setting smoothing to zero to avoid errors. Now I'm thinking about combining the base and lunar surface into a single lathe shape with a wider ground plane and a rim that steps up toward the lunar top.

Defining lathe profile coordinates...

Adding a chrome trim band and considering a 24-facet retro plinth with painted teal/cream stripes, then thinking through placing a "LUNA STATION ONE" plaque on the front face at the polygon's radius.

Either way the gap is negligible, so I'll just place the plaque facing outward along the z-axis with a plane geometry, keeping the plinth wall a bit taller to fit it comfortably. The whole base ends up around 1.36m across, which feels large for a tabletop diorama—I'm wondering if I should scale it down to something closer to 0.4m instead.

Since this represents a small moon base model, I'll settle on roughly 1.3m wide and tall enough for the antenna mast to reach about 0.85m, keeping the plinth radius at 0.68. Now I'm working out the layout on the regolith base: positioning the main dome near center with its drum and glass hemisphere reaching up to about 0.39m, then arranging habitat modules and other structures like the antenna and rocket around it, with the dome front facing +Z.

I'm sketching the connecting tubes between structures -- one capsule tube running toward +X to a lab module pod with a flat roof and radar/solar panels, ending in a hexagonal airlock, and another toward the back with a fuel sphere pod, plus a second smaller dome linked via tunnel, trying to keep the overall silhouette coherent as a small moon base diorama.

I want retro silver fuel-tank spheres on stands connected by piping, very 1950s sci-fi, and for the antenna I'm designing a tripod lattice mast with cross braces topped by a tilted parabolic dish and a glowing Sputnik-style beacon with whip antennas, positioned at the back right of the base.

I'm also adding a classic finned rocket at the front-left with a checkered red/white body, nose cone, landing legs, and a ladder for that Destination Moon aesthetic.

I'm placing a cute 4-wheeled rover with a bubble cab and dish near the front-right, plus a solar panel array on a pole near the lab module for retro flair. I'm also scattering rocks, a crater, and planting a teal pennant flag with a star/atom emblem instead of a national flag.

I want to add a small 1950s-style astronaut figure near the flag, built from basic shapes — a bubble helmet sphere, torso box, and legs — keeping proportions consistent with the scale I've established for the dome and rocket.

Now I'm sketching the texture list: dome glass lattice, plaque text, glowing porthole windows, flag emblem, rocket decals/lettering, dish panel paint, a radar-sweep control screen, checkered floor, and a Sputnik-style detail.

I'm rounding out the textures with an airlock hatch door, an atom emblem, solar cell grid panels, and considering pulling pre-made clockwork and glow kits for the tube hull and metal panelling to save time.

Setting up imports and paint helpers...

I'm checking paint resolution against the panelled seam tolerance, calculating texel density needed for 2.5mm seams across the roughly 3m² surface. Settling on a paintSize of 2048 to safely cover the fine regolith detailing while keeping the atlas and triangle counts manageable.

Now I'm defining the shared color palette as flat hex strings (teal, cream, coral, mustard, chrome, ink, regolith tones), keeping it under 64 colors for material efficiency, and writing a helper function to generate scattered rock formations using non-uniform scaled icosahedron geometry with randomized rotation and flat regolith coloring.

I'm also working out ground craters using lathe geometry — generating a bowl-shaped radial profile scaled by crater radius, with a darker interior and lighter rim distinguished by radial distance from center during the paint step.

I'm checking the lathe profile sits flush with the ground plane without z-fighting, then raising the crater slightly above it for clean rendering. For the regolith surface, I'm planning a mottled paint combining large-scale and fine noise for texture, plus scattered small rocks for detail.

Still writing regolith paint shader...

I'm adding a cheap trick for fine craters using cell noise to darken small pits where the id exceeds a threshold, giving subtle surface texture at low cost given the 1mm texel resolution at 2048.

Now I'm defining the plinth's paint function, banding colors by y-height into dark, teal, cream, and coral regions to match the base profile's wall and slope geometry, then moving on to building the dome's hull components starting with a lathed drum shape.

The drum needs an outer rim wall with a visible interior floor disc beneath the glass hemisphere, so I'm working out the lathe profile points that create a ring wall with a recessed floor rather than a solid cylinder.

For the surface look, I'm planning to paint the flat floor region with a checker pattern while giving the outer wall a cream panelled texture with subtle rivets, using normal direction and height to distinguish which paint applies where.

I still need to add a chrome rim band as a small swept ring around the top edge, then cap it with a glass dome built from a partial sphere using a translucent textured material.

Still writing dome texture SVG...

Writing the 3D rib geometry code...

Designing the interior scene floor: a central glowing atom-lamp pillar with orbiting tilted rings in amber, surrounded by stylized retro pine trees with layered cone canopies in green tones, plus small benches to furnish the space.

Now I'm working out how the connecting tubes link into the dome structure—figuring tube radius and height so it properly enters the glass at the right elevation, and placing a lab pod at the far end of tube A.

Working through the geometry, the glass dome's radius at the tube's height means the tube actually crosses the glass wall around x≈0.23–0.24 rather than where I'd placed it. I'll adjust the tube to end around x=0.215–0.22 with a small airlock collar flange to visually close the gap where it meets the dome.

Switching approach, I'll make the tubes as swept cylinders between two points with a circular cross-section, painted in the tube color, using low-poly faceted sides (around 12) rather than smooth shading to give that retro-futurist riveted look.

Now I'm thinking about adding ribbed bands around the tubes as a detail — small lathed rings at intervals along the tube axis to simulate segmented piping.

For portholes, I'll place flat textured circles on the tube surface facing outward, giving them a glow effect to make them read as lit windows.

The front-facing facet works since 90° is a multiple of 30°, so I'll place a porthole there facing +Z, plus another offset 30° up. Now I'm designing a helper function to build each porthole: a lathed chrome bezel ring plus a glowing disc offset slightly outward along the facet's normal direction.

For the lab pod at that offset position, I'm lathing a flattened dome roof profile for the cylinder body, sizing the wall radius so the connecting tube meets flush inside it, and adding a front-facing hatch texture plane for the door.

Actually, since the exact vertex placement is tricky, I realize decals solve this cleanly—projecting textures directly onto the built surface. I'll use the decal API for the hatch, plaque, and emblems, conforming exactly to each target part's geometry rather than fighting polygon orientation manually.

For portholes, I'm thinking of decaling onto the tube surface too, and skipping a separate lathe bezel by just drawing the chrome ring directly into the texture alongside a glowing warm-toned interior. Since glow() makes the whole decal emissive, I want to keep the bezel colors distinct enough (cream/dark yellow) so it still reads as bright chrome rather than washing out.

Actually, I'm reconsidering splitting it into two decals — one glow texture for just the window interior and a separate non-glow ring texture for the bezel — so the bezel doesn't look oddly luminous; that bumps my texture count but keeps things visually cleaner. I'm now tallying up all the textures needed: dome, porthole glow, bezel, plaque, hatch, atom emblem, rocket text/roundel, flag, and screen for the rover/lab.

I'll also plan the number of portholes per piece (tube A: 2 front, tube B: 2, pod: 3, rocket: 3, dome drum: 4) and figure out positioning for tube B, which runs toward the fuel spheres on the right side.

Now I'm mapping out the hub junction cylinder, the three-sphere fuel cluster on tripod legs, and the connecting pipes, plus sketching the overall top-view coordinate layout starting with the dome at origin.

I'm placing the tube connections to the lab pod and fuel cluster, and positioning the antenna and mast behind the dome so the composition stays balanced without the rocket obscuring the dome from the front view.

Checking distances from center for the second sphere, then placing pipes connecting hub to spheres. I'm positioning the rover, flag, and astronaut near the front plaque area, adjusting the rocket slightly, adding a solar panel array on a pole, and scattering rocks and craters into the remaining open spaces.

Now I'm working out the rocket's geometry, defining the lathe profile for the body and engine bell as a series of radius/height points relative to its base position.

I'm also figuring out the paint scheme — a Tintin-style checkered pattern using angle and height sectors to alternate coral and cream panels, with the nose and specific body bands colored distinctly.

Working out the fin geometry...

Now I'm working out the vertical placement so fin tips stay above ground clearance, and designing four landing legs as angled rods with foot pad discs, offsetting their rotation from the fins so they don't visually overlap.

Rungs every 0.02 giving about 8 rungs for a ladder height of .17, with rails sitting just outside the body radius so there's clearance even where the body narrows lower down. Now I'm tracking the overall rocket body span from the ground up through the antenna top.

Now I'm sketching a small astronaut figure: boxy boots, capsule legs, a torso with chest panel, backpack, arms, and a sphere helmet. Rather than a complex glass bubble with a visible face, I'll simplify to a chrome-ish helmet sphere with a mustard-colored visor decal on the front.

For the flag, I'm deciding against card-based textures since they'd only render front-facing, so instead I'll use a thin box (0.1 x 0.065 x 0.003) with the flag texture applied to its faces, which solves the double-sided visibility issue simply.
